title: Venkat Bhat - Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration

segments.text: VENKAT BHAT: So while the slides are loading.
So I'm based at the University of Toronto.
I lead the AI for mental health program there.
I'm also the National Mental Health Community
of Practice lead within the Temerty Center for AI
in Medicine, which is based at the University of Toronto.
It brings together all the universities across the country.
My focus within that is mental health.
So I've been interested in this domain for many years.
I'm a psychiatrist, a clinician scientist,
and my interest has been principally
because a lot of the developments in AI
have been based upon how the human brain works.
Deep learning is cortical representation to start off,
reinforcement learning is subcortical,
and one third of my program is around reverse engineering
these systems.
I won't be going into that today.
Most of my program, 2/3 of my program,
is around automating workflows in the clinical context
in mental health.
So that's what I'll be speaking about today.
You'll see, as I present that our usual paradigm is
we identify a workflow that we're interested in where
it may be possible to automate.
We develop the automations either a single agent
or a multi-agent system.
And with a bot playing the role of the end user,
we essentially show with a sandbox environment
and simulations that it actually works well.
And then what may be different from some
of the talks and presentations you've seen today.
I'm a clinician.
I'm a clinical trialist.
I run a lot of clinical trials.
I want to see if these things, which
in the virtual environments or simulation setup tends to
seems to work.
Does it really work in actual clinical care?
So that's what I do quite a bit.
I run clinical trials across disciplines depression, PTSD,
anxiety on the prevention side as well,
and more recently in mental health and Alzheimer's as well.
Yeah, there you go.
So I've already introduced myself.
So those are my disclosure slides.
So everything I present today, I'll
be giving a big picture view.
I won't be getting into the details.
It's all published or it's in the public domain
or it's actually coming out in the next two or three weeks.
This is my disclosure slide.
So I'll give one or two examples.
I've already given the preface as to what we do.
We show that these single or multi-agent systems work
in a simulation environment, and then we
do clinical trials, two to three year clinical trials.
So I'll give examples in each of these contexts.
I've already mentioned this as my real interest in the domain.
One third of my program is around
the interpretability side.
I won't be getting into any of those details today.
This has been my inspiration to be in this domain for many years
now.
All my presentation today will be one or two examples along
where we have automated workflows.
So I don't need to go through for this crowd,
but I'm just presenting this that about three or four years
ago as we started realizing that we are moving into an autonomy
range, going from various levels of autonomy,
we started to think, what would this
mean in clinical care in mental health.
So if there's one slide to take home from the presentation
today, and this will be my cornerstone,
and I'll keep bringing this up a couple of times.
So this was three or four years ago,
us trying to conceptualize what could
be the role of these agents in a human in the loop
model in mental health.
So came up with this idea of collaborative assistive
semi-autonomous agents, and then trying
to see what the role of the human in that loop would be.
This is another way to look at it.
What could be some assistive capabilities,
some collaborative ones, and then some semi-autonomous ones?
I think the one example of generative AI, which
most clinicians identify with and is in use is the AI scribe.
The previous speaker was also mentioning this.
A lot of the others actually require quite a bit of evidence.
So I'm not going to go into the examples with each of them,
but I'll give you one or two to give you a flavor in all
of these four domains.
Clinical care.
So this is us automating my day-to-day clinic
with different intake agents with either a single agent
or a multiple agent through the clinical workflow
from when we start seeing the patient to when
we discharge them.
We have published on each of them,
and we are now actually working towards clinical trials.
I just want to go back.
So this is the front end and the back end of the clinic.
We run clinical trials because it's not important,
it's not enough if at that particular workflow
the agent is noninferior to the human doing the task.
There are a lot of other ecosystem changes.
This change management.
There's service redesign.
A number of other things need to happen.
So that's where we do mixed methods to see
what does it take, even if it's efficacious for this tool
to actually be adopted.
We also include cost benefit because that's also
critical factor.
So I'll give you two examples here.
This is on the clinical side.
So we know in mental health that measurement based care
makes a difference.
So this is the equivalent of blood sugar for diabetes
or your blood pressure for hypertension.
Clinicians do scale.
So patients do scales like the PHQ or the GAD-7.
For over two decades, it's been really difficult to get
these things done.
So we essentially automated taking unstructured data.
So think of your ambient scribe in some sense.
And the next step to that to actually generate the scales,
and also prompting clinicians if they have not
collected this information.
This is moving into trials through Epic at our hospital
sites.
This is a multi-agent system to do diagnostic interviewing.
So essentially, we took the DSM, the operationalized DSM,
which is the SCID.
And you see a multi-agent system there,
one which is asking the questions, another which
is overseeing it does not allow you
to move on to the next module.
And then which follows the skip logic within the SCID.
And then you have an orchestrator slash diagnoser.
And we have shown that with a bot playing
the role of the patient with all kinds of DSM
complicated diagnoses, this actually does quite well.
And it's now in clinical trials where
we're showing, where we would like to see if this is useful
or not.
In the clinical trials, we are purposefully
positioning this from mild to moderate symptoms.
We know that the person with severe psychosis
or depression or Alzheimer's is not
going to be able to use this.
So I'll move on to education.
I think everyone is worried about de-skilling
that people are going to use GPT and not
learn what they need to know.
That's a legitimate concern and needs
to be addressed in different ways.
What we have tried to do is it takes 10 years to train
a clinician, four years of medical school, four to six
years of residency training.
Can we accelerate people gaining competencies
through use of agentic AI?
So essentially, we broke down the competencies
that people are supposed to attain by the time they finished
their training.
And we looked at each competency both in Canada
and in the US, the respective boards,
and we came up with a multi-agent system here.
So we have a bot playing the role of a patient.
We have a bot playing the role of the clinician,
and with the bot playing the role of the resident,
who would want to learn skills of interviewing?
How does a resident or a medical student for that matter,
learn how to do clinical interviewing, which is
the core skill of a clinician?
By doing this repeatedly and presenting to the clinician
and getting feedback.
So essentially we simulated the whole thing
with a multi-agent system.
And we are working to have seven of the largest clinical training
programs deployed this.
One arm will do the training as they're doing now.
And the other arm will see if this augmented by what they're
doing now, would lead to people gaining their competencies
sooner, i.e. rather than taking five years to finish
your training, could you gain competencies in three or four?
In theory, this sounds at least if you
look at the system we have built, it seems to work well.
But I come as a clinical trial from a skeptical perspective
on these things, that most of these things
are not going to work, at least in the way we
think it would work.
But the few things which would work
will have a transformative effect.
So this is another variant of that, a multi-agent system
to help residents learn basic principles of psychotherapy.
So cognitive behavioral therapy, motivational interviewing.
And you have the system.
It is like you're interviewing a patient within that framework.
So I'll move on.
I'm not going to dwell on this, but I've
been over the last five, 10 years doing
a lot of systematic reviews and meta analysis.
I think I won't be doing it in a couple of years.
We will have living systematic reviews
and meta analysis with the way things are progressing.
What we've been trying to do is not end-to-end automation,
but look at specific points within the systematic review
and meta analysis pipeline, and what its role is?
It takes hours and often weeks for my research assistants
to just go through and compare where the errors are as they
pull through publications.
So this is one paper on the quantitative side.
We did the same on the qualitative side
where we do thematic analysis, and we compared the themes which
would come through qualitative analysis along with as
compared to the one with generative AI,
and we're building in some automations into this.
But the bottom line is not end-to-end still
human in the loop.
And this was with the previous versions of GPT,
but I don't think it's more different with
the current versions either.
But basically what we're showing is that up
to a certain level of complexity and within particular points
within the workflow, you are able to automate them.
This is the same with another domain, which
is, in terms of data processing, for EEG analysis.
So quality improvement.
This is my last example within this realm.
So this was during the pandemic clinicians started
doing assessments virtually.
And we wanted to know what's the nature
of the relationship between the patient
and the physician in the virtual settings?
We've gone from seeing people in-person to virtually.
So essentially, this was multimodal.
We used different data streams using unstructured data
to produce the working alliance inventory.
The working alliance inventory is the proxy
for the nature of the relationship between the patient
and the physician.
So this is gradually being moved into clinical trials.
So I'll go back to this and situating
this in my presentation again.
I've given a few examples along this agentic AI roadmap
where we're actually developing assistive agents,
collaborative agents, and semi-autonomous agents.
I have two more slides and then I'll end.
We've been also looking at various different components
of these agents being able to deliver therapy.
So these papers are published.
And what we see is that as the level of complexity increases,
so we essentially forced the agent
to be able to do motivational interviewing.
And after a certain level of complexity,
it is not able to perform.
It loses its guardrails.
This will be my penultimate slide.
So here, we've been looking at if these systems are
to independently deliver therapy,
what is the nature of the interaction,
and what is the importance of the value system within it?
So here we looked at low safety guardrails versus high safety
guardrails, and we were able to show that the safety
guardrails has a significant impact in terms
of how the agent is actually perceived.
So this is my last slide.
So we looked at what the world is doing in this domain.
And it's quite important to note that in spite
of all the possibilities for what these agents could do,
there's only one randomized control trial,
now coming to two with the TheraBot last year
with GenAI based tools.
There's a real critical need to have clinical trials,
and that's what my team is significantly involved in doing.
Thank you.
